title: Dependencies, including business as usual
blurb: Use the four dependency types, and explain how business as usual, costs, quality, risks and scope can all move a project schedule.
question: A supermarket chain plans to replace the tills in 60 stores between October and February. The plan looks fine on paper, but the retail operations director says half of it cannot happen. What dependencies has the project manager probably missed, and how could they affect the schedule?

teach.h: Nothing in a schedule stands alone
teach.body: A dependency is a relationship in which one activity relies on another activity, or on something outside the project, before it can start or finish. Dependencies exist between activities within the project, with other projects, and with business as usual (BAU). Plain English: 'we can't do this until that has happened.' Getting them right is what makes a schedule realistic; missing one is how 'unexpected' delays are born.

teach.h: The four logical links between activities
head: Type
Meaning
Example
rows: B can't start until A finishes
B can't start until A has started
B can't finish until A finishes
B can't finish until A starts
Old system runs until the new one starts
teach.caption: Finish-to-start is by far the most common. Start-to-finish is the rarest, typically seen in handovers and shift changes.
External dependencies are outside the project manager's direct control, so they need agreeing with their owners and watching closely.

teach.h: Business as usual shapes the schedule
teach.body: Projects deliver change into an organisation that is still running. BAU creates dependencies such as peak trading periods, operational staff who are only free at certain times, IT system change freezes and planned maintenance windows. The link runs both ways: project work such as training or cut-over takes people away from their day jobs, so BAU managers must agree when it happens. Involving operational managers early surfaces these constraints before the baseline is set.

teach.caption: Illustrative. The original plan ran straight through December. The BAU freeze is a dependency the schedule must work around, so wave 2 waits until January.

teach.h: Costs, quality, risks and scope all move the schedule
head: Factor
How it hits the schedule
Example
rows: Less budget, fewer resources, longer durations
Funding cut halves the install team
Failed checks mean rework and retesting
Added work needs time and new links
teach.caption: The links run both ways: a schedule change also moves costs, quality and risk exposure.

rows.label: When mapped
values: Up front, in the full network
Release level, then per time box

rows.label: Approach
values: Keep backlog items as independent as possible

teach.text: Classic confusions: start-to-start does NOT mean both activities must start on the same day, only that B cannot start before A has started. Start-to-finish is the RAREST link, not the most common. And BAU is not 'outside the project's concern': peaks, freezes and staff availability are real schedule dependencies.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define a dependency: one activity relies on another, or on something outside the project.
Name the logical links (FS, SS, FF, SF) with an example of the most relevant one.
Give BAU examples: peak periods, staff availability, system freezes, maintenance windows.
Explain how costs, quality, risks and scope changes each move the schedule.
Say what the project manager does: identify dependencies with their owners early, build them into the plan, monitor them.
Four logical links: finish-to-start (most common), start-to-start, finish-to-finish, start-to-finish (rarest).
Dependencies exist within the project and with BAU, other projects and suppliers.
BAU dependencies: peak periods, staff availability, system freezes, maintenance windows.
Costs, quality, risks and scope changes can all delay or reshape the schedule.
Hidden dependencies cause 'unexpected' delays: find them early with the people who own them.

summary: You can now name and apply the four dependency types and explain how business-as-usual activities create dependencies a schedule must respect. You can also explain how costs, quality, risks and scope changes can each move a project's schedule.

A.q: Which type of dependency is the most commonly used in project schedules?
options: Start-to-finish
Finish-to-finish
Start-to-start
Finish-to-start
A.why: Finish-to-start, where the successor cannot start until the predecessor finishes, is by far the most common logical link.

whyNot.0: Start-to-finish is the rarest link type.
whyNot.1: Finish-to-finish is used, but much less often than finish-to-start.
whyNot.2: Start-to-start is common for overlapping work but is not the most used.

A.q: On a software project, testers can begin designing test scripts once development has begun. Which dependency type is this?
options: Start-to-start
Finish-to-start
Finish-to-finish
Start-to-finish
A.why: Test design can start once development has started, so the start of one depends on the start of the other: start-to-start.

whyNot.1: Finish-to-start would mean testing waits until development has finished.
whyNot.2: Finish-to-finish links the two finish points, not the starts.
whyNot.3: Start-to-finish means a successor cannot finish until a predecessor starts.

A.q: Which of the following is an example of a business-as-usual dependency for a project?
options: Testing that follows the build activity
A retailer's peak-season change freeze
A work package assigned to a supplier
The sponsor's approval of the business case
A.why: A change freeze during a retailer's peak season comes from ongoing operations, so it is a BAU constraint the project schedule must work around.

whyNot.0: That is a logical link between two project activities, not a BAU dependency.
whyNot.2: Supplier work is an external dependency, but it is not business as usual.
whyNot.3: Business case approval is a governance step, not an operational BAU activity.

B.q: A publisher's proofreading cannot be completed until the copywriting is completed. Which dependency type applies?
options: Start-to-start
Start-to-finish
Finish-to-finish
Finish-to-start
B.why: The finish of proofreading depends on the finish of copywriting: finish-to-finish. The two can overlap, but one cannot end before the other.

whyNot.0: Start-to-start links the two starts, not the finishes.
whyNot.1: Start-to-finish would mean proofreading cannot finish until copywriting STARTS.
whyNot.3: Finish-to-start would prevent any proofreading until copywriting is completely finished.

B.q: A bank's old payroll system must keep running until the new system has started live operation. Which dependency type does this describe?
options: Start-to-finish
Finish-to-start
Start-to-start
Finish-to-finish
B.why: The old system cannot finish until the new one starts: the finish of one depends on the start of the other, which is start-to-finish.

whyNot.1: Finish-to-start would mean the new system can't start until the old one stops, risking a gap in payroll.
whyNot.2: Start-to-start links the two starts, not the old system's finish.
whyNot.3: Finish-to-finish links two finish points, not a start and a finish.

B.q: Midway through a project the client adds three new management reports to the scope. What is the most likely effect on the schedule?
options: None, as reports are produced after closure
Activities are removed to keep the end date
New activities and links that may move dates
Only the cost changes, not the timescale
B.why: Extra scope means extra activities, which bring new dependencies and resource demand. Unless they fit within float, they may push the end date out, so they go through change control.

whyNot.0: Reports in scope are project deliverables and must be scheduled before closure.
whyNot.1: Removing other work is a possible decision, but not the automatic effect of adding scope.
whyNot.3: Scope changes usually affect time as well as cost.

C.q: A hospital's new imaging equipment fails its acceptance inspection and must be reconfigured. How does this quality problem most directly affect the schedule?
options: It lowers the cost of the next activity
Rework and retesting delay successors
It converts the activity to start-to-start
It frees resources for other activities
C.why: Quality failures mean rework and repeat testing. Activities that depend on acceptance cannot start until it passes, so dates move, especially if the activity is critical.

whyNot.0: Rework adds cost; it does not reduce the cost of later work.
whyNot.2: A failed inspection does not change the type of logical link.
whyNot.3: Rework ties resources up for longer rather than freeing them.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical business-as-usual dependency that could affect a project schedule?
options: A year-end IT system change freeze
Staff needed for peak operations
A planned maintenance shutdown
The format of the highlight report
C.why: The format of a highlight report is a communication choice, not an operational activity that constrains when project work can happen.

whyNot.0: System change freezes are a classic BAU constraint on implementation dates.
whyNot.1: Operational staff being busy at peak times limits when they can support the project.
whyNot.2: Planned shutdowns can block or enable project work, so they are BAU dependencies.

C.q: After several 'unexpected' delays caused by other teams, a project manager wants to prevent this on the next project. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Add a large buffer to every single activity
Map dependencies early with the owners of BAU
Avoid scheduling any work near busy periods
Ask the sponsor to cancel competing projects
C.why: Hidden external dependencies are found by working with operational managers and other project owners during planning, then building them into the schedule and monitoring them.

whyNot.0: Padding every activity wastes time and does not reveal the real dependencies.
whyNot.2: Busy periods are only one type of dependency, and avoiding them entirely may be impossible.
whyNot.3: Cancelling other work is not the project manager's call and does not address the root cause.

reteach.title: Think of a kitchen refit
reteach.question: You are refitting your kitchen while the family still lives in the house. What has to wait for what, and what does everyday family life add to the plan?

blocks.h: Links inside the job, and links to home life
blocks.body: The plumber can't connect the sink until the units are fitted (finish-to-start). The decorator can start painting once the tiler has started on the far wall (start-to-start). The old fridge stays on until the new one is running (start-to-finish). Then there is 'business as usual': the family must still eat, the school holidays are busy, and the water can only be off while the kids are out. Those everyday constraints shape the plan just as much.

blocks.text: Life at home is the BAU of a kitchen refit: ignore it and the plan fails, even if every trade's logic is perfect.

explain.body: Four link types connect activities. Finish-to-start: B starts after A finishes. Start-to-start: B starts after A starts. Finish-to-finish: B finishes after A finishes. Start-to-finish: B finishes after A starts.

test.q: In a finish-to-start dependency between activity A and activity B, what must happen?
options: A must finish before B can start
A and B must start on the same day
B must finish before A can start
A and B must finish on the same day
test.why: Finish-to-start means the successor (B) cannot start until the predecessor (A) has finished.

whyNot.1: Same-day starts are not required by any link type; start-to-start only means B can't start before A starts.
whyNot.2: That reverses the direction of the dependency.
whyNot.3: Finish-to-finish links finishes, and even then they need not be on the same day.

explain.body: Business as usual keeps running while a project delivers change. Peak periods, operational staff availability, system freezes and maintenance windows all limit when project work can happen, and project work in turn takes people away from BAU.

test.q: Why should a project manager involve operational managers when building the schedule?
options: To hand them responsibility for the plan
To reduce the number of project activities
To find BAU constraints such as peaks
To avoid using change control later on
test.why: Operational managers know the BAU calendar: peaks, freezes, maintenance windows and when staff can be released. Involving them surfaces dependencies before the baseline is set.

whyNot.0: The project manager still owns the schedule.
whyNot.1: Their input reveals constraints; it does not reduce the scope of work.
whyNot.3: Change control is still needed for changes after baselining.

explain.body: Budget limits decide how many resources you can afford, which drives durations. Risks that materialise, such as late deliveries, delay dependent activities. Both feed straight into the schedule.

explain.h: A cost cut ripples into time

test.q: A budget reduction forces a utilities project to cut its installation crews from four to two. What is the most likely effect on the schedule?
options: Durations shorten as there are fewer people
No change, as cost and time are unconnected
Only quality is affected, never the timescale
Installation activities are likely to take longer
test.why: Fewer crews means the same work takes longer, so the installation durations extend and, if critical, so does the end date.

whyNot.0: Fewer people doing the same work usually means longer, not shorter, durations.
whyNot.1: Cost and time are closely linked through the resources the budget can buy.
whyNot.2: Quality may suffer too, but the timescale is directly affected.

explain.body: Iterative teams map dependencies at release level, then deal with the detail in each time box. They keep backlog items as independent as possible and use priorities to order dependent items, so a slipping dependency changes what is in the time box, not its end date.

test.q: How does an iterative team typically handle dependencies between backlog items?
options: Fix every dependency in a network up front
Order items by priority and keep them independent
Extend the time box whenever a link is found
Ignore them, as iterative work has no links
test.why: Iterative teams minimise dependencies between backlog items and use prioritisation to order the ones that remain, keeping each time box fixed.

whyNot.0: Full up-front network logic is a linear approach.
whyNot.2: Time boxes are fixed; scope flexes instead.
whyNot.3: Dependencies still exist in iterative work and must be managed.
